Detecting early-stage esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and precancerous lesions is critical for improving survival. Here, we conduct whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) on 460 cfDNA samples from patients with non-metastatic ESCC or precancerous lesions and matched healthy controls. We develop an expanded multimodal analysis (EMMA) framework to simultaneously identify cfDNA methylation, copy number variants (CNVs), and fragmentation markers in cfDNA WGBS data. cfDNA methylation markers are the earliest and most sensitive, detectable in 70% of ESCCs and 50% of precancerous lesions, and associated with molecular subtypes and tumor microenvironments. CNVs and fragmentation features show high specificity but are linked to late-stage disease. EMMA significantly improves detection rates, increasing AUCs from 0.90 to 0.99, and detects 87% of ESCCs and 62% of precancerous lesions with >95% specificity in validation cohorts. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal analysis of cfDNA methylome for early detection and monitoring of molecular characteristics in ESCC. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly detected at a late stage, which limits survival and treatment options. Here, the authors utilise whole genome bisulfite sequencing to create a cfDNA framework to detect cfDNA methylation, copy number variants and fragmentation. Subject terms Tumour biomarkers Oesophageal cancer DNA methylation https://doi.org/10.13039/501100001809 National Natural Science Foundation of China (National Science Foundation of China) 82030089 82188102 82272938 Liu Jiaqi Liu Zhihua https://doi.org/10.13039/501100005090 Beijing Nova Program 20220484059 Liu Jiaqi issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Limited 2024 Introduction Esophageal cancer (EC) is one of the most prevalent gastrointestinal malignancies and the sixth leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide 1 . Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), the predominant histological subtype of EC, accounts for approximately 88% of new EC cases, with the majority occurring in Eastern and Central Asia 2 . ESCC exhibits a dismal prognosis characterized by one of the lowest 5-year overall survival rates (18.5% and 36.9% in the US and China, respectively) 3 , which is largely attributed to late-stage diagnosis 4 . In contrast, early-stage ESCC, such as intramucosal ESCC, and precursor lesions like intraepithelial neoplasia (IEN), can achieve nearly 100% five-year disease-specific survival rates through endoscopic en bloc resection, obviating the need for systematic treatment 5 – 7 . Therefore, early detection is critical for enhancing the survival and quality of life for ESCC patients. The gold standard for diagnosing ESCC and its precursor lesions remains endoscopy with iodine staining 8 . However, the widespread adoption of endoscopic screening faces challenges, including low compliance and the substantial cost of conducting endoscopic examinations for millions of eligible individuals in high-risk regions like China 9 . Liquid biopsy methods, capable of detecting circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) within cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in plasma, offer a promising avenue for non-invasive early cancer detection 10 , 11 . However, few studies have assessed the utility of liquid biopsy in ESCC diagnosis 12 . Advancements in cfDNA biology, coupled with the exponential growth in data volume, have enabled the detection of tumor-specific alterations with unparalleled precision, encompassing genetic 13 , epigenetic 14 , and fragmentomic features 15 . In a recent multi-omics analysis of cfDNA within the Circulating Cell-free Genome Atlas (CCGA), whole-genome cfDNA methylation emerged as the most promising signal for cancer detection, outperforming fragmentation features and genetic variants 16 . However, there are still some challenges with methylation-based approaches for detecting ctDNA. First, the intrinsic value of genetic variants (e.g., copy number variants; CNVs) and fragmentation features (e.g., fragment size) embedded within whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) data has been underappreciated 17 . A concurrent analysis of cfDNA methylation markers, genetic variants, and fragmentation features within a single WGBS dataset is needed. Second, given the pivotal roles of both genetic and epigenetic aberrations in the transition from precancerous lesions to ESCC 18 – 20 , the mutual complementarity and combined performance of these multi-omics features remain unclear. Third, the biological significance of cfDNA methylation markers and their utility for subtyping and prognosis are largely unknown. Here, we conducted WGBS on 460 cfDNA samples from 230 patients with non-metastatic ESCC or precancerous lesions and 230 matched healthy controls (HCs) from multiple centers. To simultaneously examine the cancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs), CNVs, and fragmentation features within cfDNA WGBS data, we developed a comprehensive approach termed Expanded Multi-Modal Analysis (EMMA). This approach allowed us to profile the complementarity, temporal dynamics, and detection efficacy of epigenetic and genetic features within cfDNA for ESCC. Eventually, we determined the biological relevance of optimal cfDNA methylation features in this context.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Early detection and progression of Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (ESCC) and precancerous lesions (IEN/HGIEN); ESCC molecular subtyping; ESCC tumorigenesis, cancer cell invasion, immune evasion, treatment resistance, and metastasis.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The Expanded Multi-Modal Analysis (EMMA) framework integrates cfDNA methylation, copy number variants (CNVs), and fragmentation markers from whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) data. This approach profiles the complementarity and temporal dynamics of epigenetic and genetic features in cfDNA for ESCC. CfDNA methylation markers are associated with molecular subtypes and tumor microenvironments. The ESCC-cfMeth score, derived from 40 hypomethylated and 10 hypermethylated differentially methylated regions (DMRs), reflects malignant ratios. Specific genes like ZNF132, a tumor suppressor, show promoter hypermethylation and down-regulation, while oncogenes like FLT1, LINC00680, and ID1 exhibit gene body hypomethylation and upregulation, influencing cancer cell invasion and ESCC progression. Recurrent CNVs, including amplifications and deletions, are identified in cfDNA and tissues, correlating with tumor progression and involving genes such as FBXO32 and FOXA1, which are linked to late-stage cancer events. The presence of a higher proportion of shorter cfDNA fragments (FSRs) in ESCC patients is consistent with tumor cells releasing shorter fragments, and cancer-derived cfDNA is enriched in regions with optimal DMRs located within selected FSR regions. DNA methylation serves as a stable biomarker, with aberrant patterns specific to disease progression found in early and pre-invasive lesions. Regions with CNVs show higher intratumor DNA methylation heterogeneity, indicating a strong link. The 50 DMRs classify ESCC patients into methylation-dominant, -moderate, and -poor groups. The methylation-dominant group is characterized by the CCA subtype, enrichment in cell division pathways, more epithelial cells, fewer immune cells, and better survival, with a high rate of CNVs due to active cell cycle. The methylation-poor group is enriched in immune-related pathways and the IM subtype, which tends to respond to immunotherapy. DNA methylation states are also associated with differential gene expression in ESCC tissue, with specific genes upregulated in methylation-dominant versus methylation-poor clusters.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: CfDNA methylation markers demonstrate high sensitivity across all ESCC stages, including early and precancerous lesions, and are the earliest and most sensitive for detection. In contrast, CNVs and fragmentation features (FSRs) are more linked to late-stage ESCC. ESCC-cfMeth scores were significantly higher in ESCC patients than healthy controls and increased in precancerous lesions (IENs) but did not show further increases with ESCC stage progression, suggesting their primary utility for early-stage diagnosis rather than monitoring disease progression. Conversely, CNV event rates gradually increased from high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia (HGIEN) and positively correlated with cancer stages and grades, indicating a dose-response with disease progression. The EMMA model's detection rates improved with increasing disease stage, showing 62% for IENs, 78% for stage I, 83% for stage II, and 93% for stage III ESCCs. CfDNA methylation markers generally outperform CNV and fragmentation markers, especially in early stages and precancerous lesions. Patient classification into methylation-dominant, -moderate, and -poor groups based on 50 DMRs represents a gradient of methylation intensity, with distinct molecular and survival characteristics observed in the methylation-dominant group.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The EMMA framework consistently achieves >95% specificity in validation cohorts for detecting ESCC and precancerous lesions. Both CNVs and fragmentation features show high specificity, with CNV events in cfDNA exhibiting 98-100% specificity among healthy individuals. The ESCC-cfMeth score (50 optimal DMRs) demonstrated the highest discriminatory power in distinguishing malignant from benign plasma samples. The 50 DMRs used in the ESCC-cfMeth model confirmed ESCC-specificity across 81 common cell types. Recurrent CNV regions were specifically analyzed in cfDNA to retain ESCC tissue information. No significant differences were found in gender, age, stage, tumor location, or grade among methylation-defined groups, nor in somatic mutation rates in TP53 and APOBEC genes or APOBEC mutational signatures, indicating these methylation markers are specific to methylation-driven subtypes rather than general mutation patterns or clinical features.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Untreated patients with non-metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (ESCC) or precancerous lesions (e.g., Intraepithelial Neoplasia (IEN), High-Grade Intraepithelial Neoplasia (HGIEN/stage-0 ESCC)), and age- and gender-matched healthy controls. This includes individuals in high-risk regions for ESCC, Chinese ESCC patients (from CHCAMS and Shanghai Chest Hospital), and patients across varying cancer stages.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Early detection is critical for enhancing survival and quality of life for ESCC patients, potentially leading to nearly 100% five-year disease-specific survival for early-stage ESCC and precursor lesions, addressing the dismal prognosis of late-stage diagnosis. The findings enhance the early detection and diagnosis of ESCC. ESCC-cfMeth scores and CNVs provide significant diagnostic utility for ESCC and precancerous lesions. Specific genes (ZNF132, FLT1, LINC00680, ID1) associated with DMRs are functionally relevant in ESCC development and progression, while CNV-associated genes (e.g., FBXO32, FOXA1) are linked to prognosis and late-stage cancer events like immune evasion, treatment resistance, and metastasis. The cfDNA methylation markers are potential biomarkers for molecular subtyping of ESCC and can guide therapeutic decision-making, including predicting and monitoring immunotherapy responses. The methylation-dominant group is associated with better survival outcomes, particularly in grade-II ESCC, while the methylation-poor group is associated with the IM subtype, which tends to respond more effectively to immunotherapy. This leads to improved diagnostic capability for ESCC and precancerous lesions, with the potential for increased 5-year overall survival rates through early detection and intervention, and dynamic monitoring of molecular characteristics.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility for early detection, diagnosis, and monitoring of ESCC and precancerous lesions (IEN/HGIEN). Prognostic utility for ESCC, with CNV-associated genes and methylation subtypes indicating disease progression or better survival outcomes (e.g., methylation-dominant group). Adverse risk/progression indicators include upregulation of FLT1, LINC00680, ID1, and CNV events correlating with cancer stages and grades. Therapeutic guidance through molecular subtyping can predict immunotherapy response (e.g., IM subtype) and potentially increase 5-year overall survival rates.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: CfDNA methylation markers are considered the earliest and most sensitive, with whole-genome methylation-based cfDNA analysis identified as the most sensitive method for cancer detection. The EMMA framework significantly improves detection rates, accuracy, and performance, demonstrating superior diagnostic capabilities compared to single-modal models and the ESCC-cfMeth score alone. The ESCC-cfMeth score showed high reliability with AUCs of 0.90, 0.89, and 0.87 in discovery, external, and precancerous validation cohorts, respectively, and corresponding accuracies of 82.33%, 85.00%, and 78.00%. CNVs identified in tissue WGS data were largely confirmed in tissue WGBS (72.68% amplifications, 88.22% deletions) and partially in cfDNA (38.19% amplifications, 17.17% deletions), with high specificity in healthy controls. Expression changes of key genes (ZNF132, LINC00680) were validated in an independent stage-I ESCC dataset. The 50 DMRs demonstrated ESCC-specificity, and their classification into methylation groups showed consistent associations with molecular subtypes, tumor microenvironment components, and gene expression pathways, supporting their reliability. Models underwent rigorous evaluation, including 10-fold cross-validation and iterative parameter tuning. Limitations include the relatively small size of validation cohorts, unknown potential function of multimodal markers in precancerous lesions, potential damage to cfDNA fragments during bisulfite conversion (attenuating CNV and fragmentation signals), and unreliable mutation calling in WGBS data. Individual FSRs had limited discriminatory abilities (AUCs = 0.54 and 0.53) when used alone.
recommended_alternatives: Expanded Multi-Modal Analysis (EMMA) combining cfDNA methylation markers, copy number variants (CNVs), and fragmentation features within cfDNA WGBS data for enhanced detection performance.
Utilizing cfDNA methylation markers as superior to CNV and fragmentation markers, especially for early stages and precancerous lesions.
Identifying mutations in genes like TP53 in cfDNA using additional approaches to further improve the ESCC detection rate.
Investigation of Fragment Size Regions (FSRs) associated with TP53 and APOBEC3 genes, as these regions indicate a potentially higher proportion of ctDNA in cfDNA.
Further validation of survival benefits and prognostic significance of ESCC-cfDNA and the EMMA model in large-scale real-world cohorts.
Development of cfDNA-based detection strategies tailored to individuals at varying risks across different cancer stages by understanding the complementarity and timing of cfDNA features.
